Decarbonization staircase

A sample furnace on a pellet burden, every case solved by the blast furnace decarbonization model. Cost is the works basis per tonne of hot metal (tHM). Each tab shows one view. Change the prices or the capital counted and every tab reprices.

Read me first

What this is. The results of a physics-based blast furnace model that walks one furnace from all-coke operation to the lowest-carbon configuration the model can hold: nineteen cases that differ only in what is injected, where, and through how many lances, or in one efficiency move on an injecting furnace, each solved at its own limits, and each priced on the same basis, arranged as six steps: the base case · injection and efficiency · max injection through the tuyeres only · max injection with mid-shaft assist · shaft injection and recycle · sequestration. The question it answers is the one a plant asks: what is the cheapest way down, and what does each step cost per tonne of CO₂ it removes?

The furnace. One sample furnace, 6,500 t/d of hot metal on a pellet burden, 28 tuyeres, 3,000 m³ working volume, drawn and solved from the model's own dimensions. It is not any particular plant. Every case runs on it so that the cases compare like with like.

The model. Conservation and thermodynamics first: a simultaneous mass-and-energy solve of the furnace in two segments (the matrix method of Cameron et al.), with the direct-reduction split placed by the extended operating line of Bailera et al., so that the method reaches reformed gas, top-gas recycle and shaft injection, where no rule of thumb exists. Empirical rules are used to check the conventional cases, never to constrain the solve. The model is calibrated on the literature; no plant data is in it yet, and that is the point of the last tab.

How to read the staircase. Each point is one case: its cost per tonne of hot metal against its CO₂ per tonne. The line is the staircase: from the base case to the lowest-carbon case, each step is the cheapest case that is both cheaper and lower in CO₂ than the step before. A step that cannot go down is left off the line, and the Steps tab shows what it would have cost. Captured CO₂ from the recycle cases counts as removed only when storing or selling it pays at the prices set.

What you can change. Every price (coke, PCI coal, natural gas, oxygen, power, a carbon price, a storage credit, transport) on the Prices tab, with a US deck and an illustrative European one as presets, and the capital items counted on the Capital tab. Every tab reprices as you move them. The physics is not re-solved when prices move: a large price change could move a case's cheapest oxygen level or injection rate, so read a far-off price as a guide.

The cases, by letter

A the base case: all-coke on a 1,100 °C hot blast, the highest blast temperature that keeps the flame inside its 2,200 °C ceiling at standing steam, with the burden distributed (a lower gas efficiency) so that the top gas stays at the 110 °C drying floor, the way an all-coke furnace is actually run · B, C pulverized coal at 100 and 200 kg/tHM · Q, R, S, T, V the efficiency moves of step 2, each one lever from case B: Q the hot blast raised to 1,250 °C · R the furnace's heat losses cut 15 % · S the top pressure raised 180 → 230 kPag · T a dry blast, steam 15 → 5 g/Nm³ · V a cleaner pellet, gangue −30 % (SiO₂ 4.5 → 3.1 %) · D the most coal the furnace will take, through two lances · E, F natural gas at 50 and 100 kg/tHM · G gas at 100 kg through two lances · H the most gas the furnace will take · I reformed gas from an autothermal reformer at 100 kg/tHM, the step-2 option · J the most reformed gas the furnace will take · K natural gas on one lance and reformed gas on the other · L coal with top-gas recycle to the tuyeres and the shaft (the ULCOS-class oxygen furnace) · M the most gas the furnace will take with recycle to the shaft to keep the stack warm · P the most coal the furnace will take with the same mid-shaft recycle assisting the stack. L stored and M stored are L and M with their captured CO₂ stored. Oxygen enrichment and the burden profile are chosen per case to make it feasible at the least cost; where a case says "most", the model walked the rate up until a limit it computes stopped it, and the Cases tab names that limit.

Efficiency moves the model cannot yet show. Four were probed on case B and found to be model builds rather than fuel levers, so they are reported here and not plotted. Coke quality (CSR 62 → 68, CRI 25 → 22) moved the coke rate by exactly nothing and only the bed (the fluidization index 0.61 → 0.56, fewer coke fines): the plant's 0.5 to 1 kg of coke per CSR point comes from solution loss and the thermal reserve zone answering the coke's reactivity, which the solver's fixed carbon demand does not carry. Top pressure is plotted (S) but is the same kind of lever here: +50 kPa bought 0.3 kg of coke through the coal's burnout and a fifth of the bed's headroom (0.61 → 0.50), while the stack-side gain of a high top pressure (indirect reduction improving with the gas's residence) is not in the model, whose shaft efficiency is a specification. The other two: charging 50 kg/tHM of scrap moved coke only 1.6 kg, because the two-segment solver hands every atom of iron to the lower segment as wustite and the scrap's metallic iron never reaches the coke-setting balance (the literature class is 10 to 15 kg; the fix is a metallic-iron stream into the lower segment); and dense-phase coal conveying moved nothing at all, because the carrier gas reaches neither the solve nor the flame in this model. Both are on the build list.

What the numbers are, and are not

  • Costs are per tonne of hot metal on a works basis: annualized capital, fuels, purchased oxygen and power, less the export gas sold as power. Carbon policy sits on top of that, not inside it. Units are metric; prices are US dollars.
  • CO₂ is the furnace's own, per tonne of hot metal: what leaves the furnace gate as top gas burnt or vented, net of what the recycle cases capture when storing it pays. Upstream emissions (coke making, pellets, gas supply, the oxygen plant's power) are not in it.
  • The sample furnace, the material analyses and the prices are literature-class placeholders with stated bands; a plant replaces them with its own. The ranking of the cases has proved robust to the prices; the spreads between them have not.
  • The model is under active development. Some cases carry a "previous epoch" mark where they were last solved on an earlier version of the model and are being re-solved; the Cases tab shows it.

What we would like from you

If you run a blast furnace, the tab takes your furnace's construction and one base operating period, checks that the numbers close, and prices that period on the staircase, with nothing sent anywhere. The file it writes is what the model runs to put your furnace on the staircase at its own limits. Where the model has had to assume something that a plant measures (heat losses and their split, the thermal reserve zone, the flame temperature definition, the practical oxygen ceiling, what sets your minimum coke rate), those are the questions we would most like answered, because several of them are alternative explanations for the same observations.

Where the money goes

Each case's cost per tonne of hot metal at the current prices, split into its parts. The export gas credit (top gas sold as power) sits left of zero; the dot marks the total.

Step by step

The staircase from all-coke to the lowest-carbon case at the current prices. Each step is the cheapest case in it that is both cheaper and lower in CO₂ than the step before, so the line goes down at every step it keeps. A step with no such case is left off the line, and its row shows the cheapest case in it that would cut CO₂ and what it would add. The last step always ends on the lowest-carbon case, even if it must rise in cost. Cost of CO₂ avoided = extra cost over all-coke ÷ CO₂ avoided.

Every case

The solved operating point of each case, its cost at the current prices and the limit that stopped it.

What the furnace is fed, as the model has it: the analysis each material is charged or injected with, its quality levers, and the price it is costed at. The analyses are the model's input tables (coke, pellet and fluxes typed as literature-class placeholders; the coals from NETL's published coal specifications; the reformed gas solved by the model's own reformer), and a plant replaces them with its own. The staircase cost counts coke, PCI coal, natural gas, oxygen and power; the pellet and the fluxes are priced in the deck but nearly the same in every case, so they stay outside the comparison.

What goes in, per tonne of hot metal

Fuel and reductants into the furnace, kg/tHM: coke charged at the top; coal, natural gas and reformed gas injected at the tuyeres. The pellet (about 1,560 kg in every case) and the fluxes are in the table, not the bars; ore / coke is the pellet over the coke by mass, the model’s bulk O/C (04_Slice_Model!AC213), the same figure the Furnace and Charging tabs are split by. In the recycle cases L and M the furnace also takes back part of its own top gas, which is not a raw material.

kg/tHM unless marked. Natural gas to the reformer and the reformer's oxygen make the reformed gas (cases J, K). Priced materials = coke + PCI coal + natural gas (lances and reformer) + oxygen (blast and reformer) at the current prices, the same lines as the cost build-up; the pellet and the fluxes are not in it.

The bell-less-top charging program that puts the model’s radial ore/coke profile into the furnace. The model carries the profile as eight radial bands (04_Radial_8Band: the O/C at the centre, the plateau and the wall are the case’s levers), and the Furnace tab’s layers are split by it; a plant realizes such a profile with a rotating chute, so this tab solves the chute matrix that would: eleven tilt positions, each landing on the stockline at a radius from the chute geometry, each ring a heap at the material’s angle of repose, and, for each of the two hopper dumps of ore and the two of coke that make one charge, the dump weight and the whole revolutions per position chosen together so the heaps put the model’s ore and coke masses into its bands (the flow gate is set per dump, so a light dump gives the inner bands their resolution). The section shows the chute at the positions used, the trajectories, and one charge deposited on the Furnace tab’s previous surface; the chart shows the model’s O/C by band beside what the rings deliver, with the residual; the matrix is below. Ore / coke means the pellet over the coke, by mass (04_Slice_Model!AC213, the bulk O/C the model’s profile is renormalized to), on every tab; the profile’s centre, plateau and wall levers are shape anchors, scaled to that bulk. Chute geometry, repose angles, the gate range and the dumps per charge are typical levers (stair/charging_typical.json), to be replaced by the plant’s own; the band masses are the model’s.

Charging

What is modeled: the band masses the program must deliver are the model’s radial profile at the case’s levers, and the charge batches are the model’s. The chute geometry, the trajectories, the heap rule (Jiménez 2004, Mitra 2013) and the angles of repose (Wei et al. 2022) are a typical arrangement, labelled; a plant’s own matrix and profilemeter trace replace them.

The sample furnace drawn to scale from the model's own dimensions (hearth 12 m, belly 13.5 m, throat 8.5 m, stockline 28 m above the tuyeres, 3,000 m³ working volume), with the case's solved thermal field inside it: the isotherms from the model's countercurrent shaft slice (8 radial bands × 12 slices of 2 m), the cohesive zone between the fusion-window foot (1150 °C) and the melting line (1450 °C), and the burden layers as a steady-state sketch of several hours of operation (not a dead-stacked charge): the surface from the chute’s landing ring at 0.8 of the throat radius with its slopes at the angle of repose (pellets 25°, a literature value: Wei et al. 2022; the heap rule of Jiménez 2004 and Mitra 2013), the ore and coke split by band from the model’s own radial O/C profile (the centre coke-rich), the layers descending by plug flow with their shape kept and their volume conserved across the widening shaft (Park 2011), and the ore layers thinning to nothing across the cohesive zone while the coke slits keep their thickness, so they converge on the melting line. The surface shape and landing ring are levers with literature defaults until a profilemeter trace replaces them; the ore/coke split is the model’s. Point at the inside of the furnace to read the solid and gas temperatures of the model's grid. The drawing uses bands 2 to 8 and carries the second band to the centre line with zero slope: the innermost band (0.4 % of the cross-section, a 0.5 m radius) is where the slice model's radial gas blend shows — its solid runs hotter than its gas up the stack and cooler than the band beside it through the cohesive zone — so it is kept in the data, in the hover grid and in the readouts, but not drawn. Listed for the slice port. The slice carries the FU-1 fix (2026-10-20): a band whose solid steps from below 1150 °C to above 1450 °C between two slice centres now takes its melting heat on the slice where it crosses that window; before the fix the slice charged that heat nowhere and the band’s solid ran hotter than its own gas. Cases A, B, C, D and K are re-solved at their PT-1 point with the fix; E, F, G, H and J keep their captured fields (PT-1 left those solves unchanged and no band skips there, so the fix does not act). Case L keeps its captured field (the model cannot yet reach L’s captured operating point again; that ruling is open): its band 4 skipped the window there and is drawn from the bands either side, labelled in the readouts and the hover, with the model’s own heights beside the drawn ones. Case M’s slice has no stationary point: its outer bands sit at the window’s lower edge, where the slice switches a band’s whole melting heat on or off, so its field is one snapshot of that cycle. The “Thermal field” readout says which of these a case is. “Melting heat charged in the slice grid” is the share of the melting heat the slice charges inside its grid (5 to 28 m); less than 100 % means part of the burden melts below the bottom slice, where the drawn lines are extrapolated toward the raceway.

Furnace

What is modeled: the thermal field, the fusion window and the raceway depth are the model's; the layer geometry is a steady-state sketch: the per-band ore/coke split is the model’s radial profile, the surface shape (landing ring, angle of repose) is a literature default until a profilemeter trace replaces it, and the descent is volume-conserving plug flow on the local cross-section (Park 2011); the hearth below the tuyeres, the deadman and the liquid pool are drawn as a sketch, not solved. Elevations are metres above the tuyere centreline.

The tuyere, its two lances and the raceway, in a vertical section through one tuyere axis, drawn at the model’s dimensions for the case (tuyere bore set per case for a kinetic energy of 130–160 kW per tuyere, 120–155 mm, and 14 of the 28 tuyeres active at cases M and L; a 0.3 m nose; lance tips at their setback behind the nose; the raceway depth from the model’s coal-aware jet correlation and its height from the depth). The plume shows where the model puts the injectant’s combustion: for coal, the volatiles release in 2 ms, the oxygen is used up 0.4 m from the lance tip, and the char gasifies in CO₂ and H₂O through the raceway with the completion the model solves; what is left leaves up with the gas or into the bed, where the model partitions it. Temperatures are labelled where the model computes them: the blast at the nose, the flame (the RAFT witness), the raceway gas after the particles’ heat sink, the bosh gas the coke descends through and the coke’s own temperature as it reaches the raceway. The cohesive zone’s root is drawn where the Furnace tab’s shaft slice puts it for the case (the 1450 °C melting line, the softened ore layers above it, the dripping zone below), mapped into the section by distance from the wall. The dotted contours between the raceway’s points, the deadman’s shape and temperature and the slag and metal levels are sketches, labelled as such: the model has no raceway temperature field and no deadman model. The wall around the tuyere is drawn from the model’s own inputs where it has them (the hearth and belly diameters, the cooling and lining zone table, so the hot face bends into the bosh at the top of the tuyere band) and from a typical arrangement where it does not (the lining, stave and shell thicknesses, the tuyere cooler that holds the tuyere’s base, the tuyere body and the blowpipe), each labelled as such. Point at any part of the drawing for the numbers and the cells they come from.

Raceway

What is modeled: the raceway depth and height, the jet, the residence time, the coal’s devolatilization and char burnout, the lane velocities, the coke inflow and the fines, and the temperatures at the labelled points are the model’s own cells at the case’s solved point. The deadman, the liquid levels and the contours between the labelled temperatures are a sketch; the wall construction and the tuyere assembly are a typical arrangement until the plant’s furnace data replace them. x is metres into the furnace from the hearth wall’s hot face at the tuyere level; z is metres above the tuyere centreline.

What each case makes: hot metal, slag and top gas. Every case is solved on the Python model at its operating point on the fluxed pellet adopted on 2026-10-15 (the archive's low-silica placeholder had put the slag at 187 kg/tHM; a representative North American pellet puts the all-coke furnace at 250). At L and M the model's shaft slice settles on a small cycle rather than a point, so their figures are the cycle's values.

Slag

Analysis by mass. B2 = CaO ÷ SiO₂; B4 = (CaO + MgO) ÷ (SiO₂ + Al₂O₃). Limestone is added to hold B4 at its target. Superheat is the slag tap target ( °C) less the liquidus; viscosity is at the hearth temperature. Liquidus and viscosity come from published correlations for blast furnace slag.

Top gas

The gas leaving the furnace top, from the conservation solve. Composition is on a dry basis, as an analyzer reports it; water is given on the wet gas. η CO = CO₂ ÷ (CO + CO₂); η H₂ counts only the water made by reduction. Energy is the gas's heating value per tonne of hot metal, before the stoves take their share. In the recycle cases L and M most of this gas goes back into the furnace.

A free-body sketch of the furnace on the model’s own profile: the burden column from the stockline to the melting line (its weight at the charge’s bulk densities, the gas drag on it, and the share the wall carries by Janssen’s differential slices on the weight net of that drag), the active coke zone below the melting line (lightened by the gas drag in the dripping zone), the deadman (the Raceway tab’s cone and the hearth below the tuyeres) and the buoyancy the hearth pool puts on it. The gas drag is the model’s own stack pressure drop slice by slice (its bed and gas in each slice, cohesive slices included) on the furnace’s cross-section, split at the case’s melting line and carried up to the stockline; a chart shows where along the height it sits. Two indices: HANGING — the gas drag on the burden divided by its weight — and FLOATING — the buoyancy on the deadman divided by the load it carries, shown as a bracket from the whole column over it reaching it to none of it, with the share of the column that would float it as the headline, and Takahashi’s sitting / partly floating / floating states. The lower-zone indices from the Raceway tab sit beside them.

Furnace forces

What is modeled: the geometry, the melting line, the raceway depth, the pool depth, the deadman void fraction, the coke and ore batches, the stack and lower-zone pressure drops and the lower-zone indices are the model’s at each captured point. The bulk and liquid densities, the wall friction and lateral ratio, the liquid holdup, the pool’s slag share and the state thresholds are the tab’s levers, with their sources in the side panel. The model’s stack pressure drop is the uncalibrated placeholder the sheet flags, and its slice grid places the cohesive slices at a fixed 2.3–7 m and stops at 18.7 m, so the indices are also read with the whole drag profile scaled to a plant-typical 150 kPa bed. The model has no hearth and no stress field: this is a sketch with the model’s numbers in it.

Where the top gas goes, per tonne of hot metal and at the furnace’s production: the gas the model makes (volume, composition, temperature and chemical energy on the solver basis the cost rows use), the stoves’ share, the recycle (CO₂-stripped and dried, split between the blast tuyeres and the shaft tuyeres, with the CO₂ the VPSA takes out and the share the heater burns), the export to the power plant, and the electricity ledger: export power and a top-pressure recovery turbine against the blower and the VPSA. Steam: the blast moisture consumed, and the export’s boiler-steam alternative. The conversions are the deck’s own constants (the Prices tab’s sliders carry through); the TRT and the boiler are sketches on the tab’s levers, labelled.

Gas balance

What is modeled: the top-gas volume, composition, temperature and energy, the recycle streams, the captured CO₂, the POX heater’s oxygen and burnt share, the wind and the blast moisture are the model’s at each captured point. The stove firing, the export’s power value, the blower and the VPSA use the deck’s constants (EC-1). The TRT and the boiler steam are sketches: the model carries neither; their levers and sources are in the side panel.

Your own furnace and one base operating period, beside the sample furnace. Every field starts as the sample furnace (the dashboard’s case B: PCI 100 kg at air blast, 6,500 t/d on a pellet burden), so change only what differs. As you type, the page (1) checks the numbers with conservation arithmetic only, no model physics: the iron balance, the carbon balance on the nitrogen tie (every N₂ in the top gas came in with the blast or the fuels, which sizes the dry gas), the oxygen balance with hydrogen, and the slag balance, each with the measurement it points at when it does not close; (2) prices the base period on the staircase at the prices on the Prices tab, from your own consumptions, with the CO₂ at the furnace gate from the carbon in; (3) draws the furnace to scale beside the sample furnace with its tuyeres, stockline and cooling zones; and (4) writes a file the model runner loads to solve your furnace at its own limits and walk it up the staircase. Nothing is sent anywhere: the entries stay in this page until you download the file or save them for yourself. Metric units; the model’s own cells are named in the record where a field maps to one.

Your furnace

Checks on the base period

Conservation only. A balance that does not close points at a measurement, not at the furnace: one balance flags a problem but cannot name the meter, and a second period at a different operating point usually separates them.

On the staircase

Your base period priced as the sample cases are, at the prices on the Prices tab and with the capital items counted on the Capital tab (the base furnace plant and, where you inject, the PCI plant or the gas supply). The point also appears on the Staircase tab once you have changed a field.

To scale

Your furnace beside the sample furnace at one scale: the shell from your diameters and elevations, the stockline, the tuyeres, and the cooling zones as bands on the wall (point at a band). The volume drawn is the profile’s volume to the stockline, to compare with the working volume you stated.

The file for a model run

What is computed here: balances and readouts from your entries, by conservation, and the works-basis cost by the page’s own recipe. What is not: coke rate, flame temperature, top gas temperature, permeability and the staircase steps for your furnace, which need the model; the file carries your entries to it.

How the cost is built

Works basis = annualized capital + coke + injectants + purchased oxygen + blower power + VPSA power − the export gas credit. Annualized capital is the sum of the capital items a case needs, as ticked on the Capital tab; unticking an item, such as a plant you already own, leaves it out of every case. The export credit is the top gas left after firing the stoves, sold as power. Reformed gas is priced as its inputs: natural gas to the reformer and its oxygen. Captive oxygen is not modelled; oxygen comes over the fence at the price set on the Prices tab.

Carbon policy sits on top: a price on CO₂ emitted, and for the recycle cases a credit on captured CO₂ that is stored, less transport and storage. Captured CO₂ leaves the plant only when the credit plus the carbon price beats transport and storage. Set transport and storage below zero to model CO₂ sold for use (enhanced oil recovery, chemicals): the sale value, net of transport, then counts as income. The page still counts sold CO₂ as not emitted by the furnace; whether it is avoided overall depends on the use, and the storage credit may not apply to it.

Each point is a solved operating point of the model at its own limits, solved on the Python model from the frozen archive with the pellet of 2026-10-15. The physics is not re-solved when prices move. A large price change could move the cheapest oxygen level or injection rate of a case, so read a far-off price as a guide.

Check against the repository

At the model's own price deck, the formula on this page reproduces the repository's works-basis cost of each case: the same recipe the case sheet carried, which this page matched to 2.8e-14 when the sheet last held these cases (A427). Since the pellet change the operating points live in the repository's results, not on a sheet.
